listeningScripts.title: Booking a Photography Workshop
listeningScripts.text:
Organiser: Good morning, Northlight Photography Workshops.
Caller: Hello, I'd like to book a place on one of your weekend courses.
Organiser: Certainly. Can I take your name?
Caller: It's Sylvester Okonjo. Okonjo is O-K-O-N-J-O.
Organiser: And a contact number?
Caller: 07884 512 067.
Organiser: Which workshop were you interested in?
Caller: The landscape one, I think.
Organiser: How much experience do you have?
Caller: I've had a camera for about a year but I mostly use it on automatic.
Organiser: Then I'd steer you towards the foundation weekend rather than landscape. The landscape course assumes you can set exposure manually, and people who arrive without that spend the whole weekend on the basics while everyone else photographs.
Caller: That's helpful. The foundation weekend, then.
Organiser: The fee is two hundred and sixty pounds. That covers tuition and lunch on both days, but not accommodation.
Caller: When does it run?
Organiser: The next one is the fifteenth and sixteenth of June, starting at half past nine each morning and finishing about five.
Caller: What do I need to bring?
Organiser: Your camera, obviously, plus every lens you own, spare batteries and a memory card you don't mind filling. And a tripod if you have one — if you don't, we lend them, but say now rather than on the day, because we only carry eight.
Caller: I'll borrow one, please.
Organiser: Noted. Waterproofs too. We go out whatever the weather, and the light is usually better when it's poor.
Caller: Is there any preparation?
Organiser: Read your camera manual. I know how that sounds. Two-thirds of the questions I answer on a foundation weekend are answered in the manual, and the people who have read it get much more from the two days.
Caller: Fair enough. How do I confirm?
Organiser: A deposit of sixty pounds within a week, balance two weeks before. I'll email the details today.

listeningScripts.title: Youth Hostel Arrival Briefing
listeningScripts.text:
Manager: Evening, everyone, and welcome to Kestrel Bank Youth Hostel. I'm Aoife, the duty manager, and this is the arrival briefing.

Rooms first. Check-in is from four in the afternoon, check-out by ten in the morning, and the ten o'clock is firm because the rooms have to be turned round before the next group. Your key card opens the front door and your own room only.

Meals: breakfast runs seven to nine, and dinner is served at half past six, once, not on demand. If you've booked dinner and you're going to be late, tell us at breakfast — not at six, when it's cooking.

The self-catering kitchen is available all day, and the rule there is the one people find hardest: wash up immediately, not later. We have no staff to do it and a sink of other people's plates is the single thing that generates complaints here.

Quiet hours are from eleven at night until seven. This is a shared building with thin walls, and I would rather say plainly now that the commonest reason we ask someone to leave is noise after eleven, not anything more dramatic.

The layout. As you come through the front door, reception is on your right. The dining room is directly opposite, on the left. The self-catering kitchen is behind the dining room, at the western end of the ground floor. The drying room — and you will want it — is downstairs in the basement, below reception, and the boot store is next to it. Dormitories are on the first and second floors, and the lounge with the wood burner is on the first floor at the front, above the dining room.

Two last things. There is no mobile signal in the valley and the wifi reaches the lounge and reception only, which some people treat as a fault and most come to regard as the point. And if you are walking tomorrow, write your route on the board by the door and cross it off when you return, so that we know who is still out.

listeningScripts.title: Making Figures Honest
listeningScripts.text:
Tutor: Right — let's look at your figures for the housing affordability report. This first one.
Kirsten: That's the rent increase over ten years.
Tutor: And the vertical axis starts at eight hundred pounds.
Kirsten: Because all the values are above eight hundred. It fills the space better.
Tutor: It does, and it also triples the apparent size of the rise. A reader who glances at that sees rents that have roughly quadrupled; the actual increase is about forty per cent. Nothing in the chart is false and the impression is wrong.
Kirsten: So the axis has to start at zero?
Tutor: For a bar chart, essentially always, because the bar length is the message. For a line chart showing change over time it is more defensible not to, provided you say so clearly. What you cannot do is truncate silently.
Ollie: Mine's a line chart, but I've only plotted every third year.
Tutor: Why?
Ollie: It was smoother.
Tutor: That is the wrong reason, and it is worth understanding why. You chose the interval after seeing the data, which means you selected the version that supported the shape you expected. Plot every year and let it be untidy.
Kirsten: What about the pie chart on page six?
Tutor: How many segments?
Kirsten: Eleven.
Tutor: Nobody can compare eleven angles. Use a bar chart ordered by size, and if you must keep a pie, group the small categories into one labelled slice rather than pretending they are readable.
Ollie: Is there a general rule?
Tutor: One that covers most of it: before you finalise a figure, ask what impression someone gets in two seconds, then check whether that impression matches what the numbers say. Where they differ, the figure is wrong even if every value in it is right.

listeningScripts.title: Why Supply Chains Failed
listeningScripts.text:
Lecturer: I want to look at why supply chains that had worked for decades failed almost simultaneously, and to argue that the failures were not accidents but the predictable price of a design choice that had been rewarded for a very long time.

The design is familiar. Holding inventory costs money — warehouse space, capital tied up, goods that may become obsolete — so firms reduced it, coordinating deliveries to arrive shortly before use. Done well, this frees enormous amounts of capital, and for thirty years the firms that did it outcompeted those that did not. That is the important point: this was not carelessness. It was the strategy that won.

What it also does is remove slack. A system with no inventory has nothing between a disruption and a stoppage, so a delay anywhere becomes a stoppage everywhere within days. The same efficiency that reduces cost in ordinary conditions converts a local problem into a general one.

Concentration compounds it. Efficiency also rewards buying from the cheapest capable supplier, and when every firm applies that rule they converge on the same few suppliers, often in the same region. Firms that believe they have diversified frequently discover during a disruption that their three independent suppliers all depend on a single upstream plant — and that they had no way of knowing, because visibility beyond the immediate supplier is rare.

The response has been slower than the rhetoric suggests. Firms announced resilience programmes, and what most did was hold somewhat more inventory of a few critical items and map their suppliers one level deeper. Genuine duplication of supply is expensive, and it is expensive continuously while the benefit appears only during a disruption that may not arrive in the tenure of whoever authorised the cost.

That is the structural problem and it is not really about logistics. Resilience is a cost paid in every ordinary year for a benefit in an unusual one, and our arrangements for rewarding managers, valuing firms and comparing prices all measure the ordinary years. Until something in that measurement changes, the efficient and fragile configuration will keep winning, and we will keep being surprised by the same thing.
